reference.source: Manson's Tropical Diseases / WHO Guinea Worm Eradication Programme guidance
clinicalPearls: Caused by the nematode Dracunculus medinensis, acquired by drinking stagnant water containing infected copepods (water fleas, Cyclops)
The target of an international eradication programme, so cases are now rare and geographically restricted, but recognition remains important
After a prolonged incubation of about a year, the gravid female worm migrates to the skin, most often of the lower leg or foot, forming a painful blister that ulcerates
Contact of the lesion with water triggers the worm to discharge larvae, producing intense local burning that patients relieve by immersing the limb in water, perpetuating transmission
Diagnosis is clinical, based on the visible emerging worm; larvae may be seen when the ulcer contacts water
There is no reliable curative drug; management is by slow, careful extraction of the worm over days by winding it onto a stick, with wound care and prevention of secondary bacterial infection
Prevention centres on safe drinking water (filtering or treating), health education, and containment of cases to interrupt the life cycle
reference.pathophysiology: Dracunculiasis results from ingesting water containing copepods infected with Dracunculus medinensis larvae. Gastric acid frees the larvae, which penetrate the intestinal wall and migrate into the abdominal and retroperitoneal tissues where they mature and mate. Over roughly a year the fertilised female worm grows to great length and migrates through subcutaneous tissue, usually to a distal limb. There it induces a painful blister; on contact with water the worm ruptures the skin and expels motile larvae, which are ingested by copepods to complete the cycle. Most symptoms arise from the migrating and emerging worm and the intense local inflammatory and allergic response, with pain, blistering, and ulceration. Secondary bacterial infection, cellulitis, abscess, tetanus, or joint involvement can complicate the emergence, and a retained or broken worm can provoke severe inflammation.
additionalDifferentials: Cutaneous larva migrans and other migratory helminth infections
Foreign body granuloma or retained foreign material
additionalInvestigations: Clinical identification of the emerging adult worm at the skin ulcer
Microscopy of fluid expressed from the lesion for larvae after water contact
Wound assessment for secondary bacterial infection
Plain radiography, which may reveal a calcified dead worm in chronic cases
Assessment of drinking-water source and exposure history for public health action
redFlags: Secondary bacterial infection with spreading cellulitis, abscess, or sepsis
Features suggesting tetanus from a contaminated wound
Septic arthritis or contracture if a worm ruptures near a joint
Severe systemic hypersensitivity if the worm breaks during extraction
reference.prognosis: The infection is rarely fatal and the worm is ultimately expelled or extracted, but the process is protracted and disabling; prognosis is good with careful wound care, though secondary infection or joint involvement can cause lasting morbidity.
pitfalls: Pulling the worm out too quickly and rupturing it, provoking severe inflammation
Neglecting tetanus prophylaxis and secondary bacterial infection of the ulcer
Missing the diagnosis outside classically endemic areas as eradication progresses
Failing to counsel patients to avoid water contact, which perpetuates transmission
references: WHO Guinea Worm Eradication Programme guidance
management: There is no curative drug, so the mainstay is slow, careful extraction of the emerging worm by winding a little onto a stick or gauze each day over days to weeks, taking care not to rupture it
Provide meticulous local wound care with cleansing and dressing, and treat secondary bacterial infection such as cellulitis or abscess with antibiotics
Give analgesia for the intense local pain and ensure tetanus immunisation is up to date
Keep the affected limb and lesion away from drinking-water sources to prevent larval discharge and interrupt transmission
Manage complications such as septic arthritis or contracture with appropriate surgical and physiotherapy input
Notify cases to the public-health eradication programme and address the water source through filtration, safe-water provision and community education
